mcqs.question: A `ShoppingCart` class computes totals via an `if/elif` chain keyed on a `discountType` field. What's the core design problem this signals?
options: The cart's own bookkeeping code is now coupled to every pricing rule's logic, so adding a promo means editing and retesting the cart itself
if/elif chains are always slower than polymorphic dispatch at runtime
JavaScript/TypeScript classes cannot safely hold more than one field
The cart needs to be converted into a static utility class instead
mcqs.explanation: The real issue is coupling: pricing logic that changes on its own schedule is welded into the object responsible for cart bookkeeping, so every new promo risks breaking cart code and forces a retest of the whole class. Runtime performance of if/elif isn't meaningfully worse, and the fix has nothing to do with statics or field limits.

mcqs.question: You have exactly two pricing rules that haven't changed in three years and are unlikely to. Per this topic's trade-off, what's the better call?
options: Migrate to Strategy anyway, since it's always the 'correct' OOP way to branch on type
Keep the plain if/else — Strategy's extra classes and indirection aren't worth it for stable, rarely-touched variants
Delete one of the two pricing rules to avoid branching entirely
Strategy is only valid when there are 5+ variants, so it doesn't apply here regardless
mcqs.explanation: The decision rule is churn, not dogma: reach for Strategy once you're adding variants regularly or the branching function is sprawling. For two stable, rarely-touched rules, a plain conditional is simpler and just as correct. There's no fixed variant-count threshold, and deleting a needed rule isn't a real option.

mcqs.question: An `Order` object moves itself from `Placed` to `Shipped` behavior as a direct result of calling its own `ship()` method, with no external caller choosing the new behavior. Which pattern is this?
options: Strategy — a context holds an interchangeable object behind an interface
Command — because ship() is itself a request object
State — the object switches its own current behavior as part of normal operation
Observer — because other objects are notified of the change
mcqs.explanation: Strategy and State share the same structure, but the distinguishing signal is who changes the plugged-in object: here the Order changes its own behavior internally when ship() runs, which is State's defining trait. Strategy requires an external client to pick and set the implementation.

mcqs.question: `RushDeliveryFee` and `ExpressDeliveryFee` are separate Strategy classes whose only difference is a hardcoded flat amount ($15 vs $25). What does this pitfall call for instead?
options: Keep both classes — one class per delivery option is always correct regardless of similarity
Merge delivery fee logic directly into ShoppingCart to avoid the extra files
Add a third DeliveryFee subclass so there's a consistent set of three
Replace both with one parameterized `FlatFee(amount)` strategy, since only a value differs
mcqs.explanation: This is strategy explosion — a class per variation even when only a number differs, not the algorithm. A parameterized FlatFee(amount) captures the real difference with one class. Keeping duplicate near-identical classes, or piling logic back into the cart, both make the code worse.
